other_side: Zitron thinks the China panic driving this edition is, in his words, "living in a child's fantasy": the feared thing — cheap Chinese open models matching premium American ones — has already happened, and nothing broke. His deeper objection is that the cheap-model fix was never a fix, because nobody sells AI at a profit; subscriptions amount to "selling $40 for a dollar", so switching models just changes who absorbs the subsidy. He reads the surging-cost story as the bill finally arriving: firms that were forced to pay the actual cost of tokens are now pulling back, which to him reveals demand as manufactured rather than organic. Whether Beijing closes the door is beside his point — an industry whose only answer to its costs is a cheaper loss-making model has no business model, and should be allowed to fail rather than protected.
truth_beneath: The single variable both men orbit is whether the true, unsubsidised cost of agentic AI can fall to a price businesses will actually pay. Both accept two facts: token costs in the agentic era are surging, with buyers capping spend or trading down; and Chinese open-weight models currently deliver near-frontier performance far cheaper. The empirical question that will resolve is whether Beijing actually restricts overseas distribution and, if it does, whether Western alternatives — Nemotron, Gemma, frontier tuning, fine-tuned specialists, routers — hold per-task costs down; the observable that settles it is enterprise per-task inference pricing over the next two quarters. The pure-worldview residue is whether cheapness reflects real efficiency gains or subsidy that must end. NLW is vindicated if costs keep falling through Western routes even without Chinese weights; Zitron if their withdrawal exposes unpayable true costs and spending contracts. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — so the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: frontier AI at list price is unaffordable for scaled agentic use. Watch whether Beijing formalises the restriction, and what happens to per-task prices.
